fixes.name: deployment.set-resources
fixes.description: Set the memory and CPU requests and limits of containers in the Deployment's pod template, which rolls out new pods. containers maps each container's name to the requests and limits to set, as Kubernetes quantities such as 512Mi or 250m; values not named stay as they are. Choose the values from the evidence: Themis checks that they are valid and that the cluster can run them, never how big they are. A limit can't be removed, and a request can't end above its limit.

root_causes.name: cpu_limit_too_low
root_causes.description: its steady CPU demand is above its CPU limit, which holds it back

root_causes.name: new_version_uses_more_cpu
root_causes.description: a recent rollout made it use more CPU than before

root_causes.name: transient_cpu_burst
root_causes.description: a short burst of CPU use that has passed or rarely hits the limit

root_causes.name: node_cpu_contention
root_causes.description: its node is short of CPU, slowing it below its limit

root_causes.name: other
root_causes.description: none of these: say what in the summary

guidance:
Raising a container's CPU limit is right when the container is throttled
at its limit for a sustained time and it hurts: cpu_throttled_at_limit is
true, cpu_usage_near_limit is true, and the pods are slow, fall behind,
fail readiness probes or time out, and the latest rollout didn't bring
it: throttling_came_with_rollout is false, as with no earlier version,
one throttled too, a rollout that changed nothing the pods run, only
labels or annotations, or this version using no more of its CPU limit
than the one before it did at the same age, or than it had come to use
by its end, so more load brought it. Without CPU figures of both
versions, it is false when this one ran unthrottled at least as long as
the one before it did. Raise the CPU
limit of the throttled container only, by enough to clear the
throttling; 1.5 times the current limit is a reasonable start. Cite
container_cpu, and the pod states, events or logs that show the harm.
Never lower a value, never touch memory, and never remove a limit.

Don't raise it, and say what you found instead, when:
- throttling_data_available is not true: without throttling figures from
  the metrics source, throttling can't be seen. Don't infer it from CPU
  use, latency or the alert alone; say the figures are missing.
- cpu_throttled_at_limit is false: the container is rarely held back, so
  the limit isn't what slows it.
- cpu_usage_near_limit is false while throttling is high: the container
  sits well below its limit and only bursts hit it; say so and leave the
  call to a person.
- throttling_came_with_rollout is true: the rollout changed what the pods
  run, and the version before this one ran unthrottled where this one is
  throttled, or used clearly less of its limit at the same age, so this
  one uses more CPU.
  Whether to roll it back is another kind of incident's call, not a raise
  here.
- throttling_came_with_rollout is unknown: nothing shows how the version
  before this one ran, such as no metrics history of its pods; say what
  is missing.
- the pods are slow but not throttled, and events point at their node:
  more limit won't give them CPU the node doesn't have.

templates.name: container_cpu
templates.description: CPU each container of the current revision uses now, in cores, and how often it was throttled over a window (default 1h), against its request and limit, and which metrics source said so. A figure the source can't give is null, with why.

templates.name: pod_states
templates.description: Each pod of the Deployment: its revision, readiness, and each container's state and last termination (where OOMKilled shows).

templates.name: rollout_history
templates.description: The Deployment's rollout progress, conditions, GitOps ownership markers, each ReplicaSet revision with its images and resource limits, and what the current revision changed from the one before it: in what its pods run, or only in their labels and annotations.

templates.name: target_events
templates.description: Recent events of the Deployment, its ReplicaSets and its pods, newest first.

templates.name: container_logs_tail
templates.description: The end of one container's logs. Defaults to the pod needing attention most, from the run that last ended.

templates.name: revision_health
templates.description: How the pods of the current revision and of the one before it ran, from the metrics source's history: when it first and last has them, their restarts and OOM kills, and their CPU throttling, each with when it first showed; and how much of its memory and CPU limits each container used on average, over the same time since each revision started, and for the one before, over its last that long. A source without history says so.

predicates.name: throttling_data_available
predicates.reason: prometheus says how often each container was throttled over 1h

predicates.name: cpu_throttled_at_limit
predicates.reason: api was throttled in 64% of its CPU periods over 1h, at its limit of 0.5 CPU

predicates.name: cpu_usage_near_limit
predicates.reason: api uses 0.495 CPU of its limit of 0.5

predicates.name: rollout_changed_the_app
predicates.reason: revision 2 changed what its pods run (the image of container api changed from example/search:4.1.3 to example/search:4.2.0)

predicates.name: throttling_came_with_rollout
predicates.reason: the metrics history has none of the pods of revision 1
